Thus Wellauer interprets it, and in the same sense the scholiast explains ἀντίτυπον [opposing] by ἐναντίον [contrary], which could be approved, unless in the strophe (v. 481) a cretic responded to εὐτυχεῖν [to prosper]. For this reason I conjectured τὸν Ζηνός ἀντίπνουν [the one who breathes against Zeus], which is a fitting epithet for Typhoeus.

which the grammarians cited in the Thesaurus vol. 1, 2 p. 1060 teach was pronounced with the rough breathing by the Attic writers, and there is no doubt that this spelling must be restored everywhere in the old Attic writers, about which I have spoken in the Lexicon Sophocleum p. 46 a. Rare examples of this spelling are found in the manuscripts of the tragedians. In Aeschylus ἥνυσεν [he accomplished] is written in M Pers. 721 726 744 748, ήνυσεν [he accomplished] without the breathing in 766. Aeschylus uses forms of this verb in the active aorist ήνυσα [I accomplished] and the middle ήνυσάμην [I accomplished for myself], and in the passive imperfect ἠνυτόμην [I was being accomplished].
In the remaining passages it is used in the sense of accomplishing or attaining,
How did such a great army on foot accomplish the crossing?
He accomplished a long journey with a great army.
so that it is possible to see what an end of evil he accomplished.
